# Backlog

Work that is real, but belongs to a later phase than the one in progress.

## Why this file exists

Project rule 6 (`docs/project-rules.md`): stay inside the current phase. Cross-phase edits are
how scope drifts and how divergences become untraceable.

But noticing a later-phase problem while inside an earlier phase is *useful* —
the context is fresh, and it is usually the only time anyone will see it. The
resolution is to write it down here and keep going, rather than either fixing it
now or losing it.

This is not a general TODO list. It is specifically for work deferred **because
of phase boundaries**, plus decisions deliberately postponed.

## Rules

1. An entry records what was observed and where. It does not schedule the work.
2. Note the phase that owns it. If that is unclear, say so — an entry with an
   uncertain owner is still worth more than a lost observation.
3. Entries move out of this file when the owning phase starts, not before.
4. If something is blocking the *current* phase, it does not belong here. Fix it.

## Format

```markdown
### B-000 — one-line summary

- **Found:**  YYYY-MM-DD, during <what you were actually doing>
- **Owner:**  Phase N (or: unclear — best guess and why)
- **Where:**  file:line, or subsystem
- **Blocks:** <what this will make harder or impossible if left> (or: nothing yet)

<What was observed, concretely enough that someone arriving in Phase N can find
it again without rediscovering it from scratch.>
```

### B-096 — inputtest asserts two behaviours that three later commits changed

- **Found:**  2026-09-06, wiring the native menu pointer (the harness had to be
  rebuilt because the round changed `sl_input_live_click`'s signature)
- **Owner:**  the native input track, as its own re-baseline commit
- **Where:**  `tools/native/inputtest.c:406-423` and `:454-461`
- **Blocks:** nothing shipping. It makes `tools/windows/inputtest.ps1` exit 1 on
  a clean tree, so the harness cannot be used as a gate until it is settled.

`tools/native/inputtest.c` was last touched at `fbcc3a48`. `src/platform/
sl_input.c` has three commits after it, and two of them changed behaviour the
harness pins:

    7936cbd0  B-071: the mouse sign default is now PER PLATFORM - +1/+1 on
              Windows, -1/-1 elsewhere. The harness asserts -1/-1 unconditionally
              ("the physical-direction convention defaults (both -1)"), which
              has therefore never passed on Windows.
    911603cc  aim mode no longer routes the mouse onto the N64 stick; look goes
              through analogTurn/analogPitch in BOTH modes and the stick stays
              neutral. The harness still asserts the old stick routing
              ("aim mode: the mouse becomes the N64 stick").
    02e88d7d  added four SDL entry points the harness did not stub, so it no
              longer linked at all. FIXED in this round's working tree - a link
              failure is not a re-baseline - along with the click signature.

14 of 80 checks fail for those two reasons. All 14 are in the gameplay
mouse-look sections; the 20 checks covering menu navigation, the wheel, the
buttons, the grab lifecycle and the new pointer/click path pass.

Deliberately NOT fixed here. Both readings are owner-validated by hand on real
hardware, and making the assertions match today's output is a re-baseline of an
accepted measurement - project rule 1 says that is its own commit
touching nothing else, not a side effect of an unrelated round. The correct fix
is to mirror `sl_input.c`'s own `#ifdef _WIN32` for the sign pair, and to
rewrite the aim section against `map_kbm`'s stated contract ("LOOK IS ONE PATH,
AIMING OR NOT"), verifying each against the notes in
`docs/decisions/native-input-signs.md` rather than against the binary's current
output.

### B-005 — replay is intermittently nondeterministic (BLOCKS PHASE 0)

- **Found:**  2026-08-18, verifying the trace harness
- **Owner:**  Phase 0 — this is the gate
- **Blocks:** everything; the gate is "byte-identical across 10 consecutive runs"

Roughly one replay in four reproduces. Same ROM, same input stream, same
machine, same configuration:

    run 3: DIVERGED at tick 1416     run 5: DIVERGED at tick 1383
    run 4: DIVERGED at tick  969     run 6: IDENTICAL

The divergence point wanders and occasionally vanishes — a race, not a fixed
miscalculation. It surfaces first as the game's own currentFrameCounter
advancing by different amounts (frameDelay in frametiming.c, derived from
osGetCount() deltas), so real elapsed time is reaching the simulation.

**Eliminated by measurement**, each ruled out in turn:

| Suspect | Result |
|---|---|
| Sampling on VI boundaries | real bug, fixed (breakpoint on currentFrameCounter) |
| State schema reading uninitialised memory | real bug, fixed (v5 validates contents) |
| `RandomizeInterrupt` | real nondeterminism, disabled, insufficient |
| `CountPerOp` / `SiDmaDuration` pinning | made it worse, reverted |
| Renderer (Glide64mk2 / Rice / LLE RDP) | all diverge |
| RSP plugin (HLE / LLE) | LLE better, still diverges |
| Dynamic recompiler | confirmed OFF by config readback |
| Speed limiter | disabled (correct anyway), not the cause |

**Next:** read mupen64plus core scheduling around VI and SP interrupts. Also
test whether host load is the variable — this machine runs other containers, so
emulation speed varies between runs.

**Method note, learned expensively:** verify at FULL recording length AND across
many runs. A 250-tick window, then a 1200-tick window, then a 2-run sample each
produced a green result that a larger sample contradicted.

### B-011 — native replay parity is ~13%, not "parity to tick 292"

- **Found:**  2026-08-24, starting the guard-parity investigation
- **Owner:**  Phase 1 (native track)
- **Where:** `tools/trace/nativediff.py`
- **Blocks:** `trace-verify --backend native` meaning anything

Every cross-backend figure carried until now was measured through an alignment
that compared nothing. `nativediff` computed an INDEX offset, but the emulator
samples hundreds of ticks at fc=0 while the stage loads and the native pump
emits none of them, so no offset lines the streams up — `--align-live` got
within ONE frame and still reported 0.0% across the board.

`--align-fc` joins on frame counter, which the native boot design guarantees is
exact across backends. Correctly aligned, `archives-sweep-agent` gives:

    player     240/1874  (12.8%)
    props      240/1874  (12.8%)
    chrs       37 distinct — 0 always, 18 partially, 19 never

Checked for artifact before believing it: the emulator carries 2-3 samples per
frame (only 293 of 1874 carry one; one carries 15), so the join picks the
best-agreeing sample. That moved 12.4% -> 12.8% — sampling phase was NOT hiding
parity.

So "11 of 31 guards never match" was never a finding about guards, and "player
parity to tick 292" predates both this and the per-ROM symbol-map fix. The gap
is ~87%, which is a different and larger problem than a few stray guards.

**Hypotheses already falsified — do not retry these:**

1. *Sampling phase.* The emulator carries 2-3 samples per frame, so the join
   picks the best-agreeing one. 12.4% -> 12.8%.
2. *RNG cursor.* Direct-boot does not reproduce the menu-phase RNG state, and
   `SL_RNG_SEED` exists for exactly that. Read the emulator's seed at fc=451
   (`0000000000633807`), re-ran native with it — the shim confirmed
   `RNG state 0000000000633807` — and parity did not move: player 12.8%,
   props 13.1%. Not the cause.

**What the shape of the failure says.** Divergence is immediate: player, props
AND chrs all differ at fc=451, the FIRST compared frame. That is not accumulated
drift, it is a different initial state. Props are world objects (doors, crates,
alarms) and they differ before anything has had time to move.

The live suspicion is therefore that fc=451 is not the same MOMENT on both
sides. The frame counter is exact across backends, but the emulator reaches
frame 451 having walked the menus and loaded the level the normal way, while
native direct-boots into it. Equal counters need not mean equal progress through
level setup.

**Boot alignment falsified too.** Comparing which ENTITIES exist per frame:

    fc=451   native chrs=30  emu chrs=30   only-native=0  only-emu=0
    fc=500   identical
    fc=1000  identical
    fc=4000  native=28 emu=21, 8 only-native   <- genuine downstream divergence

At the first compared frame both sides hold exactly the same 30 characters, so
native is NOT mid-setup and the level loaded correctly. Population is right;
values are wrong.

**FOUND: the native player starts the level in the wrong place.** Player
position at fc=451, from `SL_TRACE_DETAIL=-2` natively and a direct read on the
emulator:

                    x          y         z
    native      -494.42    417.84   -1958.09
    emulator   -1940.73     -8.26   -1037.23
    delta       1446.31    426.10    -920.86

Over a thousand units out on two axes and 426 units of altitude. That is not
drift - it is a different location. With Bond misplaced from frame one, props
differ (on-screen and visibility depend on where he is), chrs differ
(perception and AI react to him), and the composite can never match. The ~87%
gap is one bug, not thirty-seven.

Note native's y is +417.84 while the emulator's is -8.26, near ground. The
emulator's current_model_pos y at that frame is 463.71 - a similar magnitude,
which is suggestive but NOT confirmed; do not build on it without checking.

**RETRACTED — that root cause was wrong (2026-08-24).** See the correction
below; pads and the intro block ARE swapped natively.

**Was claimed: the native setup swap never byte-swaps the pads array or the
intro block.**

Traced from the notes, not the loader. `Intro Block Commands.txt` gives type 0 =
spawn point; `7F0790F0 - selected spawn.txt` shows the selection depends on
current player number and player count. In solo `getPlayerCount() == 1`, so
`bondview_r.c` takes `rand_pad_index = 0` and reads:

    g_Startpad[n] = &g_CurrentSetup.pads[((SetupIntroSpawn*)intro)->index]
    start_pos.x   = g_Startpad[0]->pos.x     (X and Z only - Y comes from the stan)

So two setup reads must be correct: the intro record's pad INDEX, and the pad's
POSITION. `sl_swap_setup.c` swaps ~30 record types - every propdef variant - and
has NO swapper for either the pads array or the intro block. Both are therefore
read in cartridge byte order natively.

That accounts for the whole picture: propdefs ARE swapped, which is why the chr
population is a perfect 30/30 at fc=451, while Bond alone lands at garbage
coordinates. It also explains the altitude anomaly - with X/Z pointing nowhere
valid the stan ground lookup cannot snap him down, leaving y=417.84 against the
emulator's y=-8.26.

Hypotheses eliminated on the way, all cheaply: sampling phase, RNG cursor, boot
alignment, and stubbed placement functions (all 50 native stubs are
libultra/audio/segment symbols - no game logic).

Fix: add pad-array and intro-block swapping to the native setup pass.
`sl_swap_setup.c` is native-only (`#ifndef __sgi`), so MATCH is unaffected by
construction. Two constraints found while scoping it - neither is guesswork-safe:

1. **Intro records are NOT uniformly 32-bit.** A blanket word-swap would
   corrupt `SetupIntroCamera`, which carries `u16 lang_index[2]` and a
   `char *lang_ptr`. It needs per-type swappers, exactly the pattern the file
   already uses for its ~30 propdef records. Strides come from the walk in
   `bondview_r.c`: each case advances by its own `sizeof(SetupIntroX)`, with
   `SetupIntroEmpty` as the default, terminating on `INTROTYPE_END` (9). The
   type word must be swapped BEFORE it can be dispatched on.

2. **The pads array has no length.** `stagesetup` holds a bare
   `PadRecord *pads` and nothing counts it; `startpadcount` counts only the
   SPAWN pads the intro block references, not the array. The notes do not
   describe the setup pad list either (recorded in `doc-routing.json` under
   `not_covered`).

   Proposed derivation: `(boundpads - pads) / sizeof(PadRecord)`. Verified on
   archives - the span is 9284 bytes, exactly 211 * 0x2C.

**CORRECTION — the premise above is false.** Both constraints were solved
before I looked, and the "root cause" was a search that was too narrow. The
native setup swap does NOT live only in `sl_swap_setup.c`; the section walk is
in `prop.c` (~1200-1400) and it already covers all ten sections:

    offs[0] pathwaypoints   offs[5] ailists
    offs[1] waypointgroups  offs[6] pads       <- swapped, bounded by sl_su_next
    offs[2] intro           <- swapped, walked as the reader walks it
    offs[3] propDefs        offs[7] boundpads
    offs[4] patrolpaths     offs[8/9] pad name arrays

`sl_su_next(offs, off)` already bounds each array by the following section -
the same derivation I proposed as novel. The intro walk even carries a comment
about not blanket-swapping, because that would clobber the waygroup ID arrays
sharing the gap.

So pads and intro ARE byte-swapped, and Bond still spawns in the wrong place.
The misplacement (fc=451, native -494/418/-1958 vs emulator -1941/-8/-1037) is
REAL and still unexplained; only the explanation was wrong.

**Measured: the spawn pad is IDENTICAL on both sides.** Instrumented the
selection site in `bondview_r.c`:

    native    idx=192  pos=260.465088, 39.464409, 962.931580  stan=0xf6d39e04
    emulator  idx=192  pos=260.47,     39.46,     962.93      stan=0x801b7164

So the setup swap, the intro spawn index and the pad contents are all correct
natively. Setup data is cleared of suspicion entirely.

**And neither side's Bond is at his own spawn pad by fc=451.** The emulator's is
~3000 units away, at (-1941, -8, -1037) against a pad at (260, 39, 962). So the
pad is not the final start position - something after the spawn places him, and
that placement (or the time between it and fc=451) is where the two runs part.

Note also the asymmetry in what precedes fc=451: natively it is the FIRST pumped
frame, so no recorded input has been consumed yet, whereas the emulator arrives
there having run the level normally. Whether those are the same moment is now
the open question - and the earlier "boot alignment falsified" note was weak
evidence, since identical chr SETS show only that the level loaded, not that
both sides are at the same point in it.

**RESOLVED — the spawn is correct on both sides. I was comparing the wrong
field.**

    field                    emulator                    native
    player->pos (+0x004)     -1940.73, -8.26, -1037.23   -494.42, 417.84, -1958.09
    prop->pos   (+0xA8 ->+8)   260.47, 167.31,   962.93   260.465088, 167.314392, 962.931580
    spawn pad                  260.47,  39.46,   962.93   identical, index 192

`prop->pos` is Bond's WORLD position - `bondview_r.c` writes it straight from
`start_pos`, whose X and Z come from the pad and whose Y is pad height plus
eyeheight. Native matches the emulator to the last decimal. The spawn, the pad,
the setup swap and the placement arithmetic are all correct.

`player->pos` at struct offset +0x004 is NOT the world position - it is a
derived value (camera / room-relative). The whole "native starts in the wrong
place" line of investigation was comparing it.

**Schema implication, and the useful outcome of all this:** `state.py` hashes
`PLAYER_POS = 0x004`. If that field is derived rather than authoritative, the
player component of every trace is hashing a value whose relationship to Bond's
actual position is unclear - and `prop->pos`, which IS authoritative, is
skipped, because the props digest excludes `PROP_TYPE_VIEWER`. Worth settling
before reading anything more into player parity numbers.

Hypotheses eliminated across this investigation, all by measurement: sampling
phase, RNG cursor, boot alignment, stubbed placement functions, unswapped
pads/intro (retracted - `prop.c` swaps all ten sections), and finally spawn
placement itself.

**Measured: the simulation agrees far better than the trace reports.** Dumping
both fields per frame on both sides and joining on frame counter, over fc
451..~660 (209 frames both sides had):

    prop->pos   (Bond's WORLD position)      199/209   95.2%
    player->pos (derived; what state.py hashes) 150/209   71.8%
    the trace's bundled player hash                       12.8%

The bundled hash covers pos, model_pos, room_pos, crouch, bounce, health, dead,
armour, ammo, both hands and the seven shot registers - ONE differing field
fails the whole tick. That is why it reads 12.8% while the world position it is
supposed to be about agrees 95% of the time.

First world-position divergence is at fc=548 and it is small:

    emu 43823b88,4327507c,4470bb9f
    nat 43823b0d,4325137f,4470bbba

x 260.4651 vs 260.4648, y ~167.31 vs ~165.14. Float drift, not a structural
error - a completely different class of problem from "Bond is misplaced".

CAVEAT: 209 frames is a much shorter window than the 1874 the 12.8% was
measured over, so these are not directly comparable as run-wide figures. The
contrast WITHIN the same window is the finding, not the absolute numbers.

Actionable consequences:
1. The player hash is too coarse to localise anything. It should be split, or
   at minimum reported per-field, so a divergence names the field.
2. `PLAYER_POS` (+0x004) is derived. `prop->pos` is authoritative and is not
   hashed at all - the props digest skips `PROP_TYPE_VIEWER`. The schema is
   arguably hashing the wrong player position.
3. Native parity is materially better than the corpus-wide 12.8% suggests, and
   the remaining gap starts as small float drift rather than gross error.

**Characterised: X/Z drift, Y steps.** Per-frame world-position delta
(native - emulator):

    fc=548   dx=-0.0038  dy= -2.2382  dz=+0.0016
    fc=574   dx=-0.0038  dy= +0.0000  dz=+0.0016     y recovers
    fc=588   dx=-0.0038  dy=-55.9652  dz=+0.0016
    fc=602+  dx=+0.0000  dy=-55.9652  dz=+0.0000     persists

X and Z drift continuously but tinily - 0.0038 at magnitude 260 is roughly 128
ULP accumulated over ~100 frames. Y does NOT drift; it JUMPS, recovers, jumps
again, then holds a constant -55.97.

A persistent whole-number-ish Y offset is not numeric error, it is Bond standing
on a different floor. Y comes from `bondviewYPositionRelated(stan, x, z)` - the
stan tile under him - so the mechanism is almost certainly: tiny X/Z drift
crosses a tile boundary, a different tile is selected, and that tile's height
differs by a step.

That makes the actionable target the X/Z drift, not Y. Sub-centimetre positional
error is producing whole-floor discontinuities, which is why divergence looks
catastrophic downstream (perception, visibility and AI all key off where Bond
is) while the arithmetic is nearly right.

The build already uses -msse2 -mfpmath=sse for IEEE single semantics, which the
native-boot notes say removed one-ULP differences; 128 ULP is a different
problem - accumulation, or an operation still evaluated at a different width. Do not grep one file and conclude a whole subsystem is missing -
that error has now been made four times in this investigation.

**Do not** resume chasing individual guards until this is closed; every chr
comparison downstream of a misplaced player is meaningless.

### B-008 — savestates in the libretro recorder

**Superseded 2026-08-19 by direct-boot** (`make direct-boot`). The problem was
the menu walk before every recording; setting the g_StageNum initialiser skips
it outright and selects Agent, which is what savestates were wanted for. What
savestates would still add is resuming *mid-level*, and nothing needs that
yet. Reopen if something does.

The original entry follows, since the retro_serialize caveat is still true if
anyone wires them up later.



- **Found:**  2026-08-19, porting the record path off mupen64plus
- **Owner:**  Phase 0
- **Blocks:** nothing; it is a recording-ergonomics problem, not a correctness one

`trace.py record` carries `--state` / `--save-state` from the mupen64plus era.
Neither is wired to the libretro recorder, so both now fail loudly rather than
being silently ignored - a recording that quietly ignored the savestate you
asked it to start from would be worse than no feature.

Why it matters: without them, every recording of a late campaign level starts
at the title screen and includes the whole menu walk. Twenty-plus levels makes
that real time, and the menu portion is dead weight in every replay too.

`retro_serialize`/`retro_unserialize` do work on this core, with the same
caveat as the RAM pointer - they fail before the first `retro_run()`, so a
warm-up frame has to happen first. The care needed is that the warm-up must be
identical on the record and replay sides, which is exactly the class of
off-by-one the round trip exists to catch. Wire it, then confirm
`make trace-roundtrip` still passes when both halves start from a state.

### B-009 — harder-difficulty replays as supplementary AI coverage

**RETRACTED 2026-08-20.** The measurements below were taken on ROMs where the
difficulty never reached gameplay: the build set the MENU variable only, so
every "00 Agent" run was actually Agent. The archives figure (70 -> 246
distinct) was a different Agent run, not a harder one, and proves nothing about
difficulty. Numbers kept only so nobody cites them; redo once someone wants
the comparison.

- **Found:**  2026-08-20, testing whether Agent recordings replay usefully at 00 Agent
- **Owner:**  Phase 1 (AI regression cover), not Phase 0
- **Blocks:** nothing

Replaying an Agent recording on a 00 Agent build works, and the input does not
degenerate - Bond survived the full length on both levels tested, contrary to
the expectation that he would die in the first minute.

What it buys is different coverage, not more:

| level | distinct chrs | guard-ticks |
|---|---|---|
| depot Agent | 3 | 14,305 |
| depot 00 | 4 | 18,556 |
| archives Agent | 70 | 41,374 |
| archives 00 | 246 | 33,038 |

Archives triples its distinct characters while total guard-ticks FALL by 20% -
much higher turnover, slightly smaller live population. Depot barely moves.
So a harder replay exercises spawn/death paths harder and sustained behaviour
less.

Not worth adding to the Phase 0 gate: it doubles gate time per level and the
gate measures determinism, which Agent already proves. Worth keeping a handful
as supplementary traces once Phase 1 needs AI regression cover, chosen per
level rather than wholesale.

The far bigger lever is the recording itself. Statue churns 401 distinct
characters and depot 3 - two orders of magnitude, from how the level was
played, not from difficulty.

### B-010 — the layering check counts direct includes only

- **Found:**  2026-08-24, fixing the four new violations from the native skeleton
- **Owner:**  Phase 1
- **Where:** `tools/sightline/check_layering.py`, `docs/layering-baseline.txt`
- **Blocks:** the Phase 1 exit criterion as written could be met while
  `src/game` still cannot build headless

`check_layering.py` scans each file in `src/game/` for `#include` lines naming
an SDK header. It does not follow includes, so coupling that arrives through a
game header is invisible to it.

Measured across the 138 files in `src/game/`:

- 136 include an SDK header directly — this is what the 285 count measures
- 58 also reach `ultra64.h` through `bondgame.h`, `model.h`, `bondview.h` or
  `player.h`, each of which includes it itself

So driving the baseline to zero is real work, but reaching zero would NOT mean
`src/game` is severed from the RCP layer: every file including `bondgame.h`
still gets the OS, the RSP/RDP command interface and the VI/cartridge surface.
The gate says "the baseline count must decrease monotonically and reach zero at
the Phase 1 gate", and that can be satisfied with the coupling intact.

Two things worth deciding together:

1. Whether the headers themselves get severed (a types-only header like
   `src/sl_types.h`, which `sl_ported_asm.c` now uses, is the pattern), and
   whether the check should follow includes so the number means what the gate
   assumes it means.
2. Where native-port scaffolding lives. `sl_state_reader.c`, `sl_swap_model.c`
   and `sl_swap_setup.c` sit in `src/game/` but are not game logic — they are
   the port's data-swapping and trace-reading layer. They are counted as game
   violations because of where they are, and dropping their direct `ultra64.h`
   line would only hide that, since they include `bondgame.h`/`model.h` anyway.
   Moving them out of `src/game/` is the honest option; the native build already
   globs `src/*.c`, but objects would move between link groups and MATCH would
   have to prove itself.

### B-007 — is the libretro trace fingerprint environment-sensitive?

- **Found:**  2026-08-19, auditing what the libretro port inherited from mupen64plus
- **Owner:**  Phase 0
- **Blocks:** nothing today; would let CI and host traces be compared directly

Under mupen64plus the host and the CI container produced different state hashes
from the same ROM and input - 240 VI per 120 ticks versus 356 - with identical
package versions and byte-identical binaries in both places. Each environment
was internally deterministic; they just did not agree. So `env=host|container`
went into the fingerprint, and traces from one are refused against the other.

That difference was almost certainly an artifact of VI-keyed sampling.
`retro_run()` executes exactly one frame with no VI boundaries involved, so the
mechanism should not exist under libretro. **Should is not measured**, and this
session produced nine premature root-cause claims from exactly that kind of
reasoning, so `env=` stays in `libretro_fingerprint()` until someone checks.

The asymmetry justifies the conservative choice: refusing a valid comparison
costs a re-record, while allowing an invalid one reports an environmental
artifact as a bug in the game - the failure this harness exists to prevent.

**To settle it:** capture the same level and input on the host and inside the CI
container, with `SL_ENV` forced to the same value on both so the fingerprint
does not block the comparison, and diff. Identical means `env=` can come out.
Needs the ROM mounted read-only into the container, which is permitted on this
hardware but is a container the developer starts, not the agent.

### B-006 — port the harness to libretro/parallel_n64

- **Found:**  2026-08-18, after B-005 proved mupen64plus intermittently nondeterministic
- **Owner:**  Phase 0
- **Blocks:** nothing — this is the path forward

All preconditions verified by measurement:

| Requirement | Result |
|---|---|
| Determinism | 5 runs @600 frames, 3 @2000 frames — all identical, no tuning |
| Memory access | `retro_get_memory_data(SYSTEM_RAM)` = 8 MB |
| Byte order | same 32-bit word swap as mupen64plus |
| Game runs | frame counter advances ~1 per `retro_run()`, cleanly |
| Input | reaches the game |

**Gotchas, each of which cost probes:**

- The RAM pointer is NULL until after the first `retro_run()` — cores allocate
  lazily. Fetch it after one frame, not at load.
- A button HELD from frame zero does nothing at all: 21744 presses returned,
  hash byte-identical to no input. Menus respond to the press EDGE, and a button
  already down at boot never produces one. Input streams must be replayed as
  transitions, not levels.
- `mupen64plus_next` fails to load under a minimal frontend; `parallel_n64`
  works. Not investigated further since parallel_n64 is the accuracy-focused one.
- The core declares 109 options including `parallel-n64-pak1..4`
  (`none|memory|rumble|biosensor`, default `none`). GoldenEye probes the
  controller pak — on mupen64plus a MEMPAK/NONE mismatch between record and
  replay diverged at tick 1 — so this must be pinned identically for both.

**Port scope:** `emu.py` only. The trace format, schema v5, diff engine, 23 unit
tests, CI and make targets are all emulator-agnostic. Input moves from the C
plugin to `retro_set_input_state`; recorded streams need translating from N64
`BUTTONS` bits to libretro button IDs plus `RETRO_DEVICE_ANALOG` axes — a
translation, so existing recordings stay usable.

`retro_run()` advancing exactly one frame removes the entire sampling problem:
no breakpoints, no VI boundaries, no boot-phase filtering.

**Resolved 2026-08-19.** Port complete: `make trace-roundtrip` records with a
scripted pad and replays the logged stream, and both 600 and 2400 frames come
back byte-identical (`66d5ea64...` / `c35875bd...`), frame counters included.
Green in CI on the host runner (tasks 50 and 52).

The last bug before that was worth writing down, because it will bite again:

> **One libretro core per process.** `dlopen` returns the SAME library instance
> for a path already loaded, so a second `LibretroEmulator` does not boot — it
> inherits the first one's globals, mid-run. An in-process record-then-replay
> test therefore reported a divergence that did not exist, and kept reporting it
> through three unrelated "fixes", because replay was resuming the recorder's
> core at frame 386 with the counter frozen.

What finally located it was printing the frame counter from BOTH sides rather
than only the state hash. `record fc 0..384 / replay fc 386..386` named the
cause in one line; three rounds of hypothesising from a bare "DIVERGED" had
named nothing. The harness now reports frame counters alongside state on any
round-trip failure, and distinguishes the two failure modes explicitly —
misaligned loops versus genuinely different behaviour — because they need
completely different fixes.

`LibretroEmulator` now raises `SecondCoreError` on a second construction, with a
message naming the remedy, and two unit tests hold that guard in place.

### B-004 — WSL2 ships no joystick drivers

- **Found:**  2026-08-18, attempting controller passthrough for trace recording
- **Owner:**  Phase 0 (recording), and anyone who tries this again
- **Blocks:** recording input traces inside WSL

Confirmed empirically, not assumed. `usbipd` attaches the controller and the
kernel enumerates it (`045e:0b12`), but all three interfaces report
`bInterfaceClass=ff` (vendor-specific GIP) with no driver bound. This kernel has
no `input/joystick/` directory at all and no `xpad`; `xboxdrv` fails with
"couldn't find matching endpoint" because it speaks XInput, not GIP.

Fixing it needs a custom WSL2 kernel with `CONFIG_JOYSTICK_XPAD` — the source
ships in microsoft/WSL2-Linux-Kernel but is not compiled in. Microsoft calls
keeping such a kernel current "a rather large maintenance burden".

Decision: record on Windows instead. Replay never needs a controller, so this
only ever affected where a human sits while recording.
