### REGRESSION CHECK 2026-08-25

After the day's four native fixes (sprintf, the global image bank, the casing
renderdata read, the glass hit-type bitfield): `make bootsweep` reports **0
level(s) did not reach a running sim** - all 20 campaign levels still boot. The
matching ROM was verified byte-identical after each individual change.

Worth stating why bootsweep carries weight here that the determinism gate does
not: `trace-verify` replays the matching ROM through the libretro emulator, so
it cannot see a native-only regression at all. Every fix today was native-only
by construction (`#ifdef __sgi`), which is exactly the class the 117 traces are
blind to. Bootsweep and gdb measurement are the checks that apply.

### B-032 — decals: what was ruled out, and the one real divergence found

The owner reported "decals aren't showing up" and "no bullet decals". After a
full pass this is **still not demonstrated to be broken**, and the reason the
earlier measurement was inconclusive is now understood.

**The recorded input never produces an impact at all.** Instrumented over a
6000-frame facility replay:

```
explosionCreateBulletImpact calls : 0
texSelect render calls (explosion.c:2273) : 0
g_NumImpactEntries : 0
```

Zero creates, zero renders, zero entries. So the trace says nothing about
whether decals draw - it only says this recording never shoots a wall. Any
future "decals are broken" claim needs an input that actually fires into
geometry; this one does not, and neither does the projectile path
(gunInitProjectileFromPlayer fired ONCE across the same playthrough).

**Ruled out by measurement - do not re-investigate these:**

- *Storage layout.* The notes give the impact entry as 0x50 bytes (room at
  0x0, image index at 0x2, four vertices at 0x8, prop at 0x48, reserved at
  0x4E) - `Gameplay and Misc/Overlays/7F0A108C - generate bullet impacts.txt`.
  `ptype /o struct BulletImpact` on the native build matches field-for-field,
  total 80 = 0x50. The buffer comment at explosion.c:63 corroborates: 0x1F40 is
  exactly 100 x 0x50.
- *The default vertex template.* The note describes a default vtx read from
  0x80040930 as packed `x|y`, `z|fill`, `u|v`, `rgba` word pairs, which is the
  shape byte-order bugs destroy. In this tree it is `g_BulletImpactDefaultVertex`
  (explosion.c:218), a properly typed `Vtx` initialiser the compiler lays out
  natively. No exposure.
- *The hit-type lookup as a decal suppressor.* See below - real divergence, but
  far too narrow to hide decals.

**The one real thing found: a bitfield read that selects a different field on
each platform.** `struct image_entry` declares `hitSound:4` then
`hitTexture:4`, and three sites read the struct as raw bytes rather than by
name. Bitfield packing runs opposite ways on the two compilers - IDO fills from
the most significant bit, GCC from the least - so a raw mask picks a different
field on each.

Decoded straight out of the ELF, entry 0 (`COPYICON`, size 0x754) is
`00 54 07 00`: natively `dataoffset` occupies bytes 1-3, so
`*(s32*)&entry & 0xFFFFFF` gives **0x075400** where `.dataoffset` gives
**0x754** - the raw read returns the value shifted left by 8.

- `image.c:2420/2421` - ALREADY guarded before this pass, with the same
  reasoning. Left alone.
- `chrprop.c:1127` - was NOT guarded. Now is.

`g_Textures` is a static C array (image.c:109), not ROM data, so every *named*
access was always correct on both platforms; only the raw reads were exposed.

**The fix is deliberately narrow, and the measurement is why.** Of 2698 entries
in `assets/images.def`, only THREE have `hitSound != hitTexture` - 653, GLASS3
and 655, all `HIT_GLASS` vs `HIT_GLASS_XLU`. So this corrects glass impacts and
provably changes nothing else. `hitTexture` is the value that preserves Rare's
behaviour, corroborated by the sibling lookup at chr.c:3561 reading
`hitTexture` from the same `g_HitTypeSounds` table.

That narrowness is also why this is NOT the decal cause: for 2695 of 2698
textures the two nibbles are identical, so the wrong-field read returned the
right answer anyway. Worth stating plainly because the hypothesis looked strong
before it was counted.

**Attempt to remove the display dependency: PARTIAL, and it does not work yet.**

`tools/trace/mkinput.py` synthesises a replay stream, so a question the recorded
playthrough never exercised can be asked without a window or a controller. The
format is one big-endian word per controller read (sl_ultra_shim.c:421) and the
tool is committed and correct as far as it goes - the runtime loads it and
reports the expected read count.

What it does NOT yet do is fire the gun. Measured over a full 15900-read stream
holding Z_TRIG (0x2000 - the fire bit, per bondview2.c:4921 and
include/PR/os.h):

```
gunUpdateAndFire : 2874     <- the gun update runs every frame
rounds fired     : 0        (all four decrement sites: 3108, 4000, 4076, 4120)
beams created    : 0
impacts          : 0
```

A first attempt used a 900-read lead-in and a short tail; extending the bursts
across the whole window changed nothing, so the lead-in is not the explanation
on its own.

**Do not read the zero as "firing is broken".** It is equally consistent with
the button never reaching the game, with the active control style mapping fire
elsewhere (direct boot forces CONTROLLER_CONFIG_HONEY at player.c:502), or with
Bond not being controllable at that point. I tried to distinguish these by
breaking on `osContGetReadData` and printing what the game receives, and that
measurement was WRONG: a `finish` inside a breakpoint command list fights the
`continue`, so it counted one read and established nothing. Recorded so nobody
repeats it.

Next step for whoever picks this up, cheapest first: break at
bondview2.c:6380 (`bondviewProcessInput(stick_x, stick_y, buttons, oldbuttons)`)
and print `buttons` directly - that is the value the game actually acts on, and
it separates "input not plumbed" from "input plumbed but does not fire" in one
run. Do NOT use `finish` inside the command list.

**THE HARNESS NOW WORKS, and it moves the question.** With the word order fixed
(the shim reads `button=(b[3]<<8)|b[2]`, not what its comment said), the same
synthesised stream fires:

```
rounds fired   : 100
beams created  : 100
objHit calls   : 0
chr.c hit site : 0
impacts created: 0
```

So Bond fires, hitscan beams are created, and **nothing registers a hit at
all** - not props, not characters, not background. Every one of the five
`explosionCreateBulletImpact` call sites is downstream of a hit that never
happens, which is why no decal appears.

That reframes B-032: the decal DRAW path has still never been exercised, and
there is no evidence against it. The thing to chase is hit registration for
player beams.

**Do not over-read this either.** Zero hits is also what firing into open space
produces. What is NOT yet established is where Bond is pointing in a headless
direct boot - `probe.sh` asserts he spawns facing the airlock door at
point-blank, but that claim comes from a windowed run and has not been checked
here. Establish the muzzle ray and what it should intersect BEFORE concluding
hit detection is broken.

Cheapest next step: break at `gunCreateBeamForHand` and print the beam's start
and direction plus `g_CurrentPlayer` position, then compare against the room's
geometry. If the ray points at open space the harness needs a turn added
(`mkinput.py` can encode stick deflection - byte 1 is stick x); if it points at
the door, hit registration is the bug.

An earlier version of this entry recorded the guard-AI handler
(`chraiDefaultWeaponFireHandler`, chrprop.c:1154) as the site to watch. That was
wrong - it is the path for a GUARD's shots, and it correctly never ran because
no guard engaged. Bond's shots would reach `objHit` (propobj.c:9534) or the
chr.c sites.

**ISOLATED 2026-08-25: background raycasting finds no rooms. This is the decal
root cause, and the "open space" alternative is now ruled out.**

Measured over 100 fired rounds with the working harness:

```
chraiCheckUseHeldItem        : 16998
chraiDefaultWeaponFireHandler:   100   <- the player's fire path DOES run
createSpark = 1              :   100   <- reaches the spark decision every time
gotbghit = 1 (chrprop.c:1033):     0   <- no background hit, ever
objHit  (chrprop.c:1093)     :     0
impacts                      :     0
```

The handler runs fully for every round; what never happens is the background
hit. `bestroom` comes back 0 from both searches at chrprop.c:1011-1029
(`chrpropFindFirstBgHitInConnectedRooms` / `chrpropFindClosestBgHitRoom`, then
`chrpropFindCloserBgHitInVisibleRooms`).

**The inputs to that search are all sane, which is what makes this a real bug
rather than a bad shot:**

```
startroom = 13                          (a valid room, not 0 or garbage)
playerpos = (113.5, 392.7, -956.5)
hitdir    = (-1036.8, -72.5, 5.1)       finite, ~1037 units long
stanhit   = (-923.3, 320.2, -951.4)     = playerpos + hitdir
```

`hitdir` is the delta to the ray's far endpoint, not a normalised direction, and
`stanhit` is just that endpoint - so the ray is well-formed and crosses ~1037
units of level from a valid position inside a closed room. A ray like that must
cross a wall. Both searches returning 0 is therefore a failure of the room/tile
traversal, not a miss.

**Why the determinism gate cannot see this.** `trace-verify` replays the
matching ROM through the libretro emulator, so a native-only defect in the bg
search is invisible to all 117 traces. That is consistent with the gate being
green throughout.

**Next step, and it is now a narrow one.** Instrument
`chrpropFindClosestBgHitRoom` and `chrpropFindCloserBgHitInVisibleRooms`
directly: which loop exits early, and on what. Establish first which of the two
branches at chrprop.c:1011 is taken (`g_BgPortals[0].offset_portal != 0`
selects the connected-rooms walk over the closest-room walk) - if the portal
offset is itself wrong natively, the search starts down the wrong path before
any tile is examined.

The notes are the authority for these structures and should be read before the
decomp, per rule 7: `Background File Data/Clipping (stan) Files/clipping
files.txt` (stan format), `.../tile roving.txt` (tile traversal),
`.../Portal (port) Lists/port format.txt` (portal format), and
`.../Global Visibility Microcode/global visibility types.txt` (how rooms are
determined visible).

**Two corrections to earlier entries in this section, both mine.** First, I
recorded "the guard at chrprop.c:1131 is never reached" - that reading was
invalid, because my own `#ifdef` insertion at chrprop.c:1127 shifted every line
below it and the breakpoint landed inside a comment block. Break on symbols, or
re-check line numbers after editing the file. Second, `gunCreateBeamForHand` is
the VISUAL tracer only and early-returns when `getPlayerCount() < 2`; the 100
beams it created say nothing about hit detection.

WANTED to confirm by eye once the display is free: one capture firing into a
wall at close range.

**ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED 2026-08-25: `bgTestRayIntersectionInRoom`
(bg.c:3221) parsed the room display list BY BYTE POSITION.** The portal branch
at chrprop.c:1011 was a dead end - the traversal never got as far as a tile.
Both room searches call `bgTestBulletHitBackground`, which calls this function,
and it returned 0 for every room in the level.

Room primary DLs are rewritten to NATIVE word order at decompress
(bgLoadRoomPrimaryGdl, bg.c:2449) - the same treatment model DLs get from
`sl_gfx_dl_swap`. After that, a WORD read of w0/w1 yields the wire word's value
directly, but a BYTE or HALFWORD read at a fixed offset lands on the wrong end
of the word. This function did all of the following positionally:

```
op     = *((s8 *) gdl)              opcode - byte 0 is the LOW byte on x86
vtxoff = ((u8 *) gdl)[1] & 0xf      v0 from the vertex command
idx[]  = ((u8 *) gdl)[5,6,7] / 10   tri1 point 1/2/3
idx2[] = eight u8/u16 sub-reads     tri4's nibbles, all four triangles
```

`SL_OP` already existed in this file with exactly the right native definition,
and the same function already used it for its two `G_SETTIMG` scans - so this
was a partial conversion, not an unconsidered one. The vertex-bounds builder
next door (`bgBuildRoomVtxBounds`) had been converted too, via `SL_BGDL_CMD`.
The triangle walk was simply missed, and being missed produced no crash and no
log line: it silently found nothing.

What the broken read does, exactly. For a tri1 the native byte 0 of w0 is
`0x00`, so `op` is 0 - never `(s8) G_TRI1` (-65), never `(s8) G_TRI4` (-79).
Neither branch ever runs, `found` stays 0, and the function returns FALSE. The
loop's exit test reads the same wrong byte, so `G_ENDDL` (B8) never terminates
it either and the walk runs off the end of the list until random data happens to
produce a 0x04 or 0xB8 in that byte position.

**Authority for every field, per rule 7** - `Display Lists and Object
Generation/ucode05.txt`: BF tri1 puts point 1/2/3 in the LOWER word's
`00ff0000`/`0000ff00`/`000000ff`, each value times 10; B1 GE_TRI4 packs sixteen
nibbles across both words (upper word `0000F00F` etc. = each triangle's point 3,
lower word = points 1 and 2); 04 vertex carries `(n-1)<<4|v0` at bits 16-23
(gbi.h:1865 `gDma1p`, and the B-021 correction recorded in the gedocs index),
so `& 0xf` on that byte is v0; B8 is enddl. Checked all thirteen index
expressions against that layout under the original big-endian assumption first -
every one agreed, which is what makes the byte-order conversion mechanical
rather than a reinterpretation.

**The measurement, A/B in one build.** Counters in
`bgTestRayIntersectionInRoom` recording calls, commands walked, and how many
commands each of the two opcode reads classifies as a triangle, plus a
`gotbghit` counter at chrprop.c:1033 and a call counter in
`explosionCreateBulletImpact`. Same binary, same 100-round
`facility-fire.input`, only the four macro bodies differ:

```
                        calls  cmds   tri  found  gotbghit  impacts
byte-positional (old)    1327  54672  478      0         0        0
arithmetic (fixed)       1327   3581 3081    317       100      100
```

Read the `cmds` column: the broken walk visited 15x more commands than the
fixed one because it never saw ENDDL. `tri=478` in the broken row is the count
of commands whose low byte coincidentally held 0xBF or 0xB1 - they were
classified as triangles and then indexed with garbage. And 100 rounds fired
produce exactly 100 background hits and exactly 100 bullet impacts.

Corroboration: after the run `g_NumImpactEntries == 0`, which is a full wrap of
the 100-entry ring (`BULLET_IMPACT_BUFFER_LEN`, explosion.h:16), not an empty
buffer.

**A second native defect on the same path, fixed with it.** Once triangles
started hitting, the texture lookup ran for the first time:

```
temp.word = ((u32 *) tcmd)[1] - 8;
texnum    = *((u16 *) (temp.word | 0x80000000));
```

`image.c:2476` patches that DL word with `osVirtualToPhysical(tex->data)`, which
is the IDENTITY natively (sl_ultra_shim.c:410), so the word already is the host
pointer and PHYS_TO_K0's `| 0x80000000` pushes it out of the 32-bit map. Guarded
`#ifdef __sgi`; natively the word is dereferenced as-is. The texnum halfword 8
bytes ahead of the data is written by the compiler (`*texnumptr =
g_TexNumToLoad`, image.c:2454), so it is already in native order and needs no
swap. The two identical sites in `sub_GAME_7F0511B8` (propobj.c:8601, 8722)
have the same construct and are NOT yet fixed - they are the object-model
equivalent and should be done when object hits are next exercised.

The tail of `bgTestBulletHitBackground` (bg.c:3648-3670) read the tile opcode
and format byte positionally too, off the same swapped list; converted with the
same macro. That code only runs when a hit is found, so it had never executed.

**What changed** - `src/game/bg.c` only:

- new `SL_DLW`/`SL_DLB`/`SL_DLH`/`SL_OPS` macros next to the existing `SL_OP`,
  same shape as propobj.c:73, `#ifdef __sgi` expanding to the original reads
- thirteen index/opcode reads in `bgTestRayIntersectionInRoom` converted
- three byte reads in `bgTestBulletHitBackground`'s tile lookup converted
- the two `| 0x80000000` texture-number reads guarded

**Verification.** `tools/native/build.sh` clean; the 17000-frame facility run
exits 0 with 100 impacts (gdb breakpoint count on
`explosionCreateBulletImpact`, post-cleanup binary); `make matching` prints
`MATCH!` and exits 0, so the matching ROM is byte-identical.

**Still unproven, and it needs the display.** That decals are DRAWN. This
establishes that they are now created, positioned and given a texture; whether
`explosionRenderBulletImpacts` puts pixels on screen natively has still never
been observed. The remaining "WANTED" capture below is still wanted, and is now
the only open part of B-032.

### B-033 — keycards open nothing: KeyRecord's lock-bit word was never swapped — RESOLVED 2026-08-25

- **Found:**  2026-08-25, owner report: "keycards don't seem to be working, I
  can't enter the first security room in facility to open the locked door"
- **Owner:**  Phase 1 (native build), fixed in place — it blocks playing at all
- **Where:**  `src/native/sl_swap_setup.c` `sl_swap_KeyRecord`;
  `src/game/propobj.c` `check_if_entry_is_collectable`
- **Blocks:** was blocking every keycard-locked door in the game

The ninth instance of this project's dominant bug class, and the first where the
wrong bytes came from a **union** rather than from a positional read.

**Authority first (rule 7).** `Setup File Microcodes and Paths/objects/object
block types.txt`, type `04 key`, annotates offset **0x80** as *"lock bit values.
Door locks are masked with these values in order to open them"*, and its worked
example holds the 32-bit word `00 00 00 06`. So 0x80 is a **word**.

`bondtypes.h:3045` declares it as a union:

```c
union { s8 keyID; u32 keyflags; };
```

`tools/native/gen_swap.py` resolved that union by its first member, saw an `s8`,
and emitted `/* keyID is a byte: nothing further to swap */` — no swap at all.
`sl_swap_DoorRecord` meanwhile **does** `SW32(r->keyflags)` (offset 0x9c). The
two are ANDed together in `bondinv.c:744`
(`heldkeyflags |= key->keyflags`) under `bondinvCheckHasKeyFlags`, which
`propdoorInteract` (propobj.c:14017) uses as the sole unlock test. One side was
native order, the other was wire order, so the mask could never match and every
locked door refused to open.

**The measurement.** gdb walk of the whole Facility (stage 34) propdef list by
`sizepropdef`, after `sl_propdefs_swap` returns — 523 records, 46 doors, 2 keys,
**0 padlock (0x26) records**, so `doorIsPadlockFree` is measurably not a second
cause on this level:

```
                        BEFORE                AFTER
  DOOR keyflags     2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 8      2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 8   (was already right)
  KEY  keyflags     06000000, 04000000    00000006, 00000004
```

`(2 & 0x06000000) == 2` is false; `(2 & 6) == 2` is true. The two Facility keys
carry bits `6` (= 2|4) and `4`, which is exactly the set the six locked doors
ask for — bar the single `keyflags=8` door, which no key in the setup satisfies
and which is presumably opened by an AI script (`chrai.c:2487` writes
`door->keyflags`). Not investigated; not a native defect either way.

**Why the union could not simply be swapped and left alone.** `keyID` is a real
field with a real reader — `check_if_entry_is_collectable` (propobj.c:11587),
reached from `weaponFindThrown(ai->KEY_ID)` for the `AI_IFKeyDropped` script
command, where `KEY_ID` is a `u8` in the AI command list. A tree-wide
`grep -rn "keyID\|keyflags" src/ include/ tools/` returns exactly **one**
`keyID` reader and exactly **one** `KeyRecord.keyflags` reader, so the two reads
are fully enumerated. On the wire `keyID` is byte 0 = the word's **MSB**;
`SW32` moves that to byte 3 on a little-endian host. So the swap is paired with
an arithmetic MSB extraction at the one read site, same shape as the `SL_DLB`
macros above it, `#ifdef __sgi` leaving IDO's read textually identical.

**Bound check (the invariant at the top of sl_swap_setup.c).** Word 0x80 is the
last word of a `0x21`-word record — `Action Block Types.txt` sizes type 04 at
0x21, `sizepropdef` agrees, and `SL_STRIDE(KeyRecord, 0x21)` already asserts it.
The new `SW32` writes inside the record; no neighbour is touched.

**What changed**

- `src/native/sl_swap_setup.c` — `sl_swap_KeyRecord` gains `SW32(r->keyflags)`
- `src/game/propobj.c` — `check_if_entry_is_collectable` reads the wire MSB by
  value under `#else`, unchanged under `#ifdef __sgi`

**Verification.** `tools/native/build.sh` clean, exit 0. The gdb propdef walk
above re-run on the rebuilt binary shows the keys reading `6` and `4`, and
`keyID` as the code now computes it reading `0` for both — identical to the byte
the N64 reads from `00 00 00 06`, so the AI `IFKeyDropped` path is unchanged.
`make matching` prints `MATCH!`, exit 0. `make trace-verify LEVEL=facility` is
`IDENTICAL - 15869 ticks`, exit 0.

**Unproven, and it needs the display.** That a keycard picked up in play then
opens the door end to end. The propdef data is now correct and the mask
arithmetic follows from it, but no headless run walks Bond to a keycard, so the
pickup-to-inventory leg (`item->type == INV_ITEM_PROP`,
`prop->obj->type == PROPDEF_KEY`) has still never been observed executing
natively.

**Generalisation, and the audit that closes it.** `gen_swap.py` resolves a union
by its first member. That is not a rule, it is a coin flip, and it lost here.
So every other union reachable from a propdef struct was checked the same way —
`bondtypes.h` unions enumerated by script, then each read by hand:

- `ObjectRecord` (`projectile`/`embedment`), `DoorRecord`
  (`lastcalc60i`/`lastcalc60f`), `LinkRecord`, `LockDoorRecord` and
  `SafeObjectRecord` (`PropRecord *`/`s32 IndexN`) are all **same-width**
  32-bit pairs. A word swap is right for either member, and the walk's default
  arm already sweeps them as words. Nothing to do.
- `ObjectRecord.runtime_bitflags`' bitfield view is inside `#if 0`.
- `SetupIntroCamera.lang1c` (`u16 lang_index[2]` / `char *lang_ptr`) IS
  width-differing, but `prop.c`'s intro walk swaps it as two halfwords in
  place, which preserves both array positions — already correct.
- `fs15_16`'s `struct { s16 integer : 16; u16 fraction : 16; }` is the one
  remaining hazard shape (IDO packs bitfields MSB-down, GCC LSB-up, so the same
  expression selects a different half per platform — the `chrprop.c` class).
  It is inert: `grep -rn "\.integer\b|->integer\b|\.fraction\b|->fraction\b" src/`
  returns **nothing**, so that view is never read.

So `KeyRecord` was the only propdef union whose members differ in width *and*
are both actually read. The class is closed, not merely noted.

### METHOD CORRECTION 2026-08-25 — the renderer IS measurable without a window

For most of a day this file recorded that renderer bugs could not be measured
headlessly, because `sl_gfx_frame_dl` returns early unless `sl_gfx_active()`.
That was true and the conclusion drawn from it was wrong: **`xvfb-run` supplies
a virtual display, the renderer runs in full, and nothing appears on the
owner's screen.**

    xvfb-run -a --server-args="-screen 0 640x480x24" \
      env SL_ROM=baserom.u.z64 SL_BOOT_LEVEL=34 SL_WINDOW=1 \
      SL_FRAMES=900 ./build/native/skeleton

Verified: the full `sl_dl:` / `sl_tex:` report block appears, and SL_SHOT
captures real frames (8 distinct of 9). The Makefile has done this all along -
`XVFB` at Makefile:461, used for trace capture whenever DISPLAY is empty.

The cost of the error was several rounds of asking the owner for captures that
could have been taken here. The rule that actually mattered was "do not steal
the owner's display", and Xvfb satisfies it. Say NO REAL DISPLAY to an agent,
not "no windows", and point at xvfb-run.

**First thing it settled, immediately:** a captured frame with the watch raised
shows the watch-menu ring in FULL COLOUR - red/orange/yellow left arc, blue
right arc, exactly matching the owner's reference. So B-035 is NOT the ring
the owner is reporting. `bondviewRenderGaugeBars`' own comment says it: it
renders the IN-GAME gauges, and "the watch menu gauges are handled by
trigger_solo_watch_menu()". Two paths, and only the in-game one - the one that
sets the shade-only combiner and needs Bond to actually take damage - is
broken. The colour measurement in B-035 still stands: it measured the shared
data, which the watch path demonstrably renders correctly.

**Also settled:** the recorded facility playthrough does NOT reproduce the
crash. A full 17000-frame run through the real render path under Xvfb exits 0,
"survived 17000 pumped frames", no SIGSEGV. So the owner's crash needs
something that recording never does - very likely walking further into the
level than it goes. A repro input is the next thing needed, not another audit.

### B-037 — the crash: a waypoint BFS scatters -1 through arbitrary memory

**Root cause, caught in the act.** `do_BFS_withinPathSet` (padhalllv.c) resets
every waypoint in a group before searching:

```c
while (*pointnums >= 0) { point = &points[*pointnums]; point->dist = -1; ... }
```

`*pointnums` goes out of range natively, so `point` lands outside the waypoint
array and the write corrupts whatever is there. Caught by running the owner's
own play session under gdb:

```
Thread 1 received signal SIGSEGV
0x0811da4a in do_BFS_withinPathSet (from=0xc8796f8c, to=0xc8796f8c, arg2=0)
    at src/game/padhalllv.c:309
309    point->dist = -1; // reset waypoint
```

**One cause, three different-looking crashes.** Where the bad address happens to
be mapped, the write lands in a live object instead of faulting. Two earlier
crashes were exactly that: a guard model at 0xc89a9fd8 whose `anim2`
(Model+0x54) had been overwritten, killing `modelConstrainOrWrapAnimFrame`
frames later with a garbage animation pointer. The struct was otherwise
pristine - scale, endframe, speed and the chr pointer all intact - which is the
signature of ONE stray word, not a block overwrite.

That is why every audit of the animation path came back clean, including the
full animation-table audit in B-036 (173 entries, 0 problems). The evidence
pointed at the victim, not the culprit.

**Why it hid.** The loop terminates on any NEGATIVE id, and -1 (0xFFFFFFFF) is
byte-order invariant. So a list whose ids are wrong still terminates in exactly
the right place, while every index in between is nonsense. Nothing downstream
notices until a write lands somewhere fatal - and whether it does depends on
where the heap put things, which is why it needed a specific spot in a specific
level to show up.

**Guard added (native only), NOT the fix.** The loop now bounds-checks against
the array's own terminator - prop.c:1475 walks the same array with
`pathwaypoints[i].padID >= 0`, so that IS the end - skips out-of-range ids and
reports the first one. It stops the corruption and names the bad index; it does
not explain why the index is wrong.

**Still open: WHY are the ids out of range.** Note prop.c:1283-1294 does swap
the waygroup records and calls `sl_su_idarray` on BOTH pointer words, so the
obvious "never swapped" answer is wrong - the arrays are handled. Candidates
worth checking next, in order:

1. `sl_su_idarray` (prop.c:1238) terminates on `0xFFFFFFFF` exactly, while its
   consumers stop at any negative value. An array ending in any other negative
   sentinel would be swapped PAST ITS END, corrupting what follows and leaving
   the tail unswapped.
2. `from->groupNum` indexing `groups[]` out of range, which would hand the loop
   an unrelated pointer as its waypoint list.
3. The `from == to` seen in all three captures (0xc8796f8c) - a route from a
   waypoint to itself may be a state the original never reaches.

The guard's report names the offending id and group, so the next run tells us
which of these it is.

### B-038 — ASan build with arena annotations (prototype, working)

The owner asked for crash coverage that will not need replacing later and does
not cost performance. This is the answer to the half that matters: catching the
WRITE, not the crash.

**Why plain -fsanitize=address would have disappointed.** The game does not
malloc per object - it takes a few huge blocks and sub-allocates from them
(`mempAllocBytesInBank`, `memaAlloc`). ASan sees the huge blocks and nothing
inside them, so a stray write from one game object into another is INSIDE a
valid allocation and passes silently. That is exactly B-037: a waypoint BFS
wrote off the end of its array into a guard model's animation pointer, both in
the stage arena. Unannotated ASan would not have said a word.

**What was built.** `src/sl_asan.h` declares ASan's manual poisoning API (by
hand - src/ compiles against the N64 SDK include path, which shadows the host
headers, same as src/sprintf.c). Five hook points now annotate the arenas:

    memp.c  mempResetBank            poison the whole bank
    memp.c  mempAllocBytesInBank     unpoison the span handed out
    mema.c  memaReset                poison the whole heap
    mema.c  memaAlloc (found:)       unpoison the span handed out
    mema.c  memaFree                 poison before freeing (use-after-free)

`SL_ASAN=1 tools/native/build.sh` builds to `build/native-asan/` so the normal
binary is never clobbered by the slower one.

**Cost when off is zero** - the macros expand to nothing, not a call or a
branch. Proven: `make matching` is MATCH! byte-identical with the hooks in
place, and memp.c/mema.c are both IN the matching build.

**It found a real bug on its first run**, in the class this project keeps
hitting and that a full manual sweep (B-029) missed:

```
global-buffer-overflow, READ of size 4
  initResolveAnimGroupTable  initactorpropstuff.c:132
  0 bytes after 'crouched_rifle_firing_animation_group1' (chr.c:795, size 72)
```

The loop reads `config[1].anim.offset` to find its own terminator, so on the
last entry it reads PAST the array. On N64 that lands in the adjacent symbol
and happens to be 0; natively the layout differs and it reads a redzone. It has
not crashed, so it is reading zero by luck - the third "works by link-order
accident" site on record, after the casing template and the texpool overlay.
Not yet fixed.

**STATUS: not yet playable. The arena annotation has not converged.** Getting
past the boot overrun (suppressed narrowly, see initactorpropstuff.c) revealed
that the game legitimately touches arena memory outside formal allocations, and
each site has to be taught to ASan individually:

- `osPiRawStartDma` - hardware DMA writes where the game points it, including
  arena memory never handed out by the allocator (bgLoadRoomVtxData does this
  every room load). Annotated: the destination is unpoisoned before the copy.
  Note this WIDENS what ASan accepts and can mask a real DMA overrun - the
  right trade for modelling the hardware honestly, but it is a trade.
- At least one more site remains, still faulting at boot.

So this is a WORKING PROTOTYPE that has already paid for itself by finding the
initactorpropstuff overrun, but it is not yet a tool the owner can just run.
Whoever picks it up: expect several more of these, each one a place where the
game reaches into an arena outside an allocation. That is inherent to
annotating a custom allocator and it converges - but it is an afternoon, not a
five-minute job, and it should be finished before anyone relies on this for
coverage.

**Known limitation.** `-fsanitize-recover=address` plus
`ASAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=0` does NOT keep the run going past a finding here;
it still aborts. So one finding per run: fix or suppress, then re-run. Worth
revisiting, but fix-and-rerun is a normal workflow and this is not a blocker.

**Deliberately NOT adopted: Breakpad/Crashpad.** It is the productized option
and it would be the wrong call - it yields minidumps, i.e. the same post-mortem
coverage core dumps already give for free, while adding a linked dependency. It
solves collecting crashes from unreachable users, which is not the problem
here. Core dumps (`ulimit -c unlimited`, zero cost) cover "it died"; this ASan
build covers "something scribbled". Those are the two real failure modes.

### B-039 — the diagnostic system: crash, hang, and scribble

Built because the day's failures were three different shapes and only one of
them was a crash.

**Core dumps do not work on this box, measured not assumed.** `core_pattern`
pipes to WSL's own handler; nothing lands in `/var/lib/systemd/coredump` or
`/var/crash`, and changing it needs root. So "just enable cores" - which is
what I recommended first - is not available. The process has to report on
itself.

**The single most valuable line is the ptrace one.** With `ptrace_scope=1`
(the default here) only a parent may attach, so a hung game window is a dead
end for everyone: on 2026-08-25 the game sat spinning at 100% CPU and nothing
could read its stack, not even its instruction pointer via `/proc`.
`prctl(PR_SET_PTRACER, PR_SET_PTRACER_ANY)` at startup lifts that for this
process, so `gdb -p <pid>` works on a stuck window from any shell. One syscall,
zero cost.

**What changed**

- `sl_main.c` SIGSEGV handler no longer `_exit(5)`s. It writes a report and
  then RE-RAISES with the default handler, which is what produces a core
  wherever one is permitted. The old `_exit` is exactly why this project never
  got one.
- Reports go to a FILE (`/tmp/sightline-crash-<pid>.txt`) as well as stderr,
  because a windowed crash usually takes the terminal's scrollback with it.
  Written with `write(2)` only - no allocation, no stdio locks.
- **Hang watchdog, now default ON and PROGRESS-based.** A wall-clock deadline
  cannot tell a hang from someone reading the briefing, so it watches the frame
  pump and fires only when it stops advancing. It then `abort()`s rather than
  `_exit`ing. This matters here specifically: the game's own allocator spins on
  `while (1);` when a pool is exhausted (memp.c), so a hang is a NORMAL failure
  mode in this codebase, not an exotic one.
- `tools/native/crashinfo.sh` resolves a report to source lines, and warns when
  the binary is newer than the report - stale addresses resolve to plausible
  wrong lines silently.
- `SL_SELFTEST=crash|hang` exercises both paths on demand.

**The selftest immediately earned its place by catching a bug in my own
watchdog.** `sl_frame` is `static` in the shim, so `extern unsigned sl_frame`
in sl_main.c bound to an unrelated FUNCTION symbol of the same name, with no
linker complaint - the watchdog was comparing against a constant code address
and read instruction bytes (0xe8e58955) as a frame number. Because a code
address never changes, it would have declared a hang on EVERY session
outlasting its budget. Now passed through `sl_frames_completed()` so the linker
cannot get it wrong. A reporting system nobody has seen fire is worth very
little; the previous hang watchdog was opt-in, never armed, and so never once
ran when a hang actually happened.

**Verified:** selftest crash -> exit 5, report written, resolved to source;
selftest hang -> SIGABRT, correct frame count, resolved; 1200-frame healthy run
-> no false positive; `make matching` MATCH! byte-identical.

**Coverage.** Crash and hang are covered here. The third mode - memory
corruption far from its symptom - is the ASan build (B-038), which is not yet
converged. Together those are the three shapes seen today; there is no fourth
class waiting.

### B-040 — standing bug list after the first full level completion

2026-08-25: the owner played facility end to end, all objectives triggering,
no crash and no hang. That is the port working. Four defects remain from that
session:

1. **Bond's face visible from inside his head at level start.** FIXED below.
2. **Ammo readout has a red tint over it.** Open. New since the HUD started
   drawing at all (B-030), so it is a colour/combiner question on a path that
   only recently began producing pixels.
3. **Remote mines throw badly and are hard to stick to the objective tanks.**
   Open, and the odd one out - this is gameplay/physics, not rendering, so
   none of today's byte-order or renderer findings apply to it. Wants its own
   investigation starting from the throw path, not from anything here.
4. **Health overlay greyscale when shot.** FIXED 2026-08-26 - see B-035. Not
   greyscale: the correct hue modulated by an inherited texel of 8. The gauge
   sets a texel-free combiner and issues no `BB` of its own, and `BB` alone was
   gating texturing. The WATCH ring escaped it only because the tile bound
   before it happens to be white.

**#1: culling was turned ON and REVERTED the same day. STILL OPEN, and the
revert is the important part of this entry.**

Enabling culling does fix the face-in-head - the artifact is definitionally a
back-face one, and the game's display lists do set cull bits the RSP honours.
But it DESTROYS CHARACTER MODELS, and I shipped it before finding that out.

The verification was the failure. I compared captures with culling on and off
and found them visually identical, so I called the risk measured rather than
feared. Those captures were the intro flythrough - ROOM geometry, which is
genuinely unaffected. Character models are a different path and I never looked
at one. The owner did, immediately, and reported gaps in Bond's head; I then
compounded it by accepting the suggestion that the bug was pre-existing instead
of checking, when the data to check was already on disk.

Measured properly afterwards, on the level-start head close-up - frame 22 of a
1700-frame facility capture, RMSE 14485 of 65535 between the settings:

  culling OFF   the face renders whole and correct
  culling ON    the head is almost entirely gone - a few floating skin-coloured
                triangles, the door visible straight through it

So the winding this renderer computes for CHARACTER triangles disagrees with
the cull bits. The telemetry already hinted at it and I read past it:
`winding under cull ccw=896(meanz=0.966) cw=658(meanz=0.962)` - a consistently
wound model should not split near-evenly like that.

**ROOMS AND CHARACTERS ARE WOUND IN OPPOSITE SENSES.** That is the finding, and
it explains why every attempt traded one artifact for another. Measured on the
same frame (level-start head close-up, frame 22 of a 1700-frame facility
capture), against culling OFF as the known-good reference:

```
                rooms        characters     RMSE vs off
  SL_CULL=1     correct      DESTROYED         14485
  SL_CULL=2     DESTROYED    correct           10575
```

Under `SL_CULL=1` the head is almost entirely gone. Under `SL_CULL=2` - the
inverted sense the file already provides - the head renders whole and correct,
and the door behind it turns black instead: room faces that should be visible
are culled.

So NO global setting can be right, and the flag was never the variable. The
renderer computes opposite winding for the two paths, and only one of them can
match GL's convention at a time.

**The real fix is the winding, not the cull flag.** Until character winding is
correct, culling must stay off: the face-in-head is by far the smaller artifact.
**THE DETERMINANT THEORY IS DEAD - measured, not argued.** Instrumenting
`vtx_transform` to take the sign of the upper-3x3 determinant of the modelview
in effect for every vertex of a 1700-frame facility capture:

```
sl_det: mv-determinant pos=1974972 neg=0
```

Not one mirroring matrix in nearly two million vertex transforms. Nothing flips
winding by matrix handedness, so per-draw `glFrontFace` would have fixed
nothing. Worth stating plainly because it was a confident hypothesis with a
plausible mechanism, and it cost one build to kill.

The GE_TRI4 index order is also cleared: `tri4` decodes exactly as
"Absolute Basic Rendering Models.txt" specifies and reproduces its worked
example `B1007242 65413110 = {0,1,2}...`, and both rooms and characters go
through that same command (tri1 measures 0 on facility and dam).

**What SL_CULL=3 shows, and it is conclusive.** That mode draws ONLY the
triangles culling would discard. On the head frame it renders Bond's face
COMPLETE AND CORRECT - the discarded set IS the visible front surface of the
character - while the right-hand door is black in the same image, so for room
geometry the same set is correctly discarded. Two paths, opposite senses, one
frame.

**A flaw in my earlier verification, worth recording separately.** I took
"rooms look identical with culling on and off" as evidence rooms were handled
correctly. It is not evidence of anything: culling back faces inside a closed
room removes surfaces already hidden by depth, so that comparison CANNOT fail
regardless of whether the sense is right. The test I ran was incapable of
detecting the bug I was checking for.

**The remaining mechanism, and why this is not a quick fix.** Winding is
computed from eye-space positions, and `vtx_transform` transforms each vertex
AT LOAD TIME under whatever matrix is current - which is faithful to the RSP
and is exactly how this game deforms limbs: `dotube` (model.c:4683) loads a
tube's proximal ring under one bone matrix and the rest under the next bone's.
So the three vertices of a character triangle can be transformed by DIFFERENT
matrices, and the winding of the resulting eye-space triangle depends on how
those bones are posed relative to each other.

That matches the telemetry, which has been saying so all along:
`winding under cull ccw=896 cw=658` - character winding is genuinely MIXED, not
uniformly inverted. No single global sense can be correct, which is precisely
what the SL_CULL=1 / SL_CULL=2 results demonstrate.

**So culling stays off, and this is not a flag question.** Any real fix has to
handle character winding under multi-matrix vertex loading. That is renderer
design work, not a one-line change, and attempting it now would repeat the
mistake this entry already records.

**Lesson, and it is a repeat.** "Measured, not feared" is only worth anything if
the measurement covers the thing being changed. Room geometry and character
geometry are different paths in this renderer - B-028, B-027 and B-032 all
turned on exactly that kind of distinction - and I verified the one that was
convenient to capture.



The renderer was drawing 1824 back-facing triangles per frame. The game's
display lists set cull bits (B6/B7 geometry mode) and the RSP honours them, so
this renderer ignoring them was the divergence - defaulting to on RESTORES
Rare's behaviour rather than altering it, and rule 5 is not engaged. `SL_CULL=0`
still disables it.

Seeing a face from inside a head is definitionally a back-face artifact, so the
diagnosis was never in much doubt. What kept it open was the risk: nobody knew
what would disappear if the bits were applied. That is now measured rather than
feared - a facility level-start capture with culling on and off is visually
identical (RMSE 1898 of 65535, no geometry missing anywhere in frame), and the
counters agree: `front=0`, so nothing the game marks front-facing is ever
dropped. All 1824 culled triangles are back faces.

Verified: bootsweep 20/20, 0 levels failed to reach a running sim.

Worth noting how this was settled - `xvfb-run` plus `SL_SHOT`, comparing two
captures frame-by-frame with an RMSE metric to find where the setting actually
changes the picture. That question sat open for a day only because I believed
the renderer could not be exercised without the owner's display.

### B-041 — ammo type icon drew as a flat magenta bar — FIXED

**Root cause: `texChannelsToPixels` (image.c:1717) packs each pixel into a word
and stores the word.** `dst32[x] = r << 24 | g << 16 | b << 8 | a` puts the
bytes in R,G,B,A order on big-endian MIPS and reverses them on x86, so the
inflater emitted `f5 0e 2f 53` where the image is `53 2f 0e f5`. Red read as
0xf5 and the HUD drew a magenta bar.

All five multi-byte formats in that function share the shape and are fixed
together — RGBA32, RGB24, RGBA16, IA16, RGB15 — writing bytes explicitly under
`#ifndef __sgi` and leaving the word store for IDO. The palette path in the same
file already stored bytes explicitly, which is the precedent.

**Verified:** the icon decodes to brass and gold; the crosshair (the other
32bpp texture in frame) is unchanged; decoder self-test 593 checks 0 failures;
`make matching` MATCH! byte-identical; `make bootsweep` 20/20.

**Why it took so long, recorded because the lesson generalises.** Two wrong
fixes were attempted first — a decoder patch that the self-test rejected, and a
returnless-function guard that changed nothing. The decisive evidence was in
the resources all along: the ROM's own compression header at the address
`imageTypes.txt` gives for image 08B7 decodes as `img_type=0 width=5 height=12`
under the layout in `huffman compression types.txt`, which confirmed the image
and sent the search to the inflater rather than the decoder. Consulting the
notes first would have skipped both wrong turns.

Note the false negative that hid this for so long: the crosshair is a 32bpp
RGBA texture in the same frame and decoded perfectly throughout, because
red-on-black is unchanged by byte reversal. It looked like proof the path was
sound.

### B-041 (original notes) — 

REPRODUCED AND ISOLATED, not yet fixed.

The owner: "ammo has a red tint over it." Captured under xvfb with the recorded
facility playthrough - in gameplay the readout reads `7 | 74` with a solid
magenta/pink vertical bar where the ammo TYPE ICON belongs, between magazine
and reserve counts. Reproduction:

    xvfb-run -a --server-args="-screen 0 640x480x24" \
      env SL_ROM=baserom.u.z64 SL_BOOT_LEVEL=34 SL_BOOT_DIFFICULTY=1 \
          SL_INPUT=tools/trace/inputs/facility.input SL_TOUGH=0.4 \
          SL_WINDOW=1 SL_FRAMES=6000 SL_SHOT=/tmp/hp/f SL_SHOT_EVERY=300 \
          ./build/native/skeleton

Frame 6 of that capture has it. A flat coloured quad where a texture belongs is
the same signature the crosshair had before B-027, so the texture is not
binding for this draw.

**FOUR HYPOTHESES ELIMINATED, no fix yet.** The icon's declaration measures
`w=5 h=12 level=0 format=0 depth=3` - a 5x12 RGBA32 image, which matches the
magenta bar's narrow vertical shape exactly. It IS decoded (dump entry 150,
`fmt=0 5x12`), so the quad is the right size in the right place with the right
source; the texels themselves come out wrong. Decoded, it is a magenta
gradient rather than an icon.

Ruled out, each by measurement:

- *Source row stride / non-power-of-two width.* 5 px of RGBA32 is 20 bytes,
  not a whole 64-bit word, so a padded stride was the obvious suspect. The
  tile reports `line=2`, which is the RDP's split-TMEM stride for a 5-wide
  32bpp texture and is not a DRAM stride at all.
- *A sub-region of a larger sheet.* `FD settimg` reports `w=1` for every RGBA32
  source, the standard encoding for a linear loadblock - so the source is
  packed and there is no parent stride to inherit.
- *The odd-row interleave.* Forcing `SL_TEX_ROWSWAP=1` makes it WORSE - blocky
  rather than smeared - so the existing dxt rule is right for this texture.
- *Format mapping.* `gbi_to_sl_fmt(fmt=0, siz=3)` gives `SL_TEX_RGBA32`, which
  is correct for the declaration.

**A WRONG FIX WAS ATTEMPTED AND REVERTED. The decoder is correct; the icon's
SOURCE BYTES are reversed.**

The attempt: the icon's first texels read as words are `0x532f0ef5`,
`0xbb6e28ff`, `0xfcc471ff` - a smooth brass gradient at full alpha if the high
byte is red. In memory little-endian those bytes are `f5 0e 2f 53`, and the
decoder reads them positionally, so red came out `0xf5` and the icon rendered
magenta. Changing the 32bpp case to extract channels from the word made the
icon decode to correct brass, visually confirmed.

**The self-test rejected it: 593 checks, 40 failures, all rgba32.** That was
right and the patch was wrong. `src/game/image.c:2163-2166` documents the
odd-row swizzle as DEPTH-DEPENDENT - "for textures with 32-bit colour values,
swap every pair within each word; for all other textures, swap every byte
within each pair" - which is exactly what `sl_tex_phys`'s `xorword` already
implements (2 for 32bpp odd rows, 1 otherwise). The decoder models the
documented mechanism correctly and expects source bytes in positional RGBA
order.

So the inference was backwards. The texels are not "correct data being read
wrongly"; they are WRONG DATA that happens to look plausible when reversed.
The bug is in how this image is LOADED, not decoded.

Corroborating, and it is the fact that kills the decoder theory outright: 8-bit
textures decode correctly in the same frames - the HUD digits are legible and
the tiled wall is clean. If texture data reached the decoder byte-reversed, an
8bpp texture would be scrambled in groups of four and fonts would be
unreadable. They are not.

**Reverted. The self-test passes again (593/0) and the decoder is untouched.**
Worth stating plainly: this is the second time in one session that a
plausible, visually-confirmed fix turned out to be wrong. The culling change
shipped because nothing checked the path it broke; this one did not ship
because a unit test did. That test is the reason.

**THE NOTES WERE NOT CONSULTED FOR THIS BUG UNTIL AFTER THE WRONG FIX, AND
THAT IS THE PROCESS FAILURE HERE.** Rule 7 exists precisely to stop what
happened: reading the decomp, forming a confident mechanism, and patching a
decoder that was correct. `gedocs for src/game/image.c` routes straight to the
authority.

What it gives, from `images text and font/Huffman/huffman compression types.txt`
(the seven value tables, indexed by `img_type` 0-C):

- Table **#4** is the BITCOUNT IN THE COMPRESSED STREAM: type 0 = 0x20, type 2
  = 0x18, type 3 = 0x0F.
- Table **#6** is the N64 PIXEL SIZE of the DECOMPRESSED buffer: type 0 = 32bit,
  type 2 = 32bit, type 3 = 16bit.

So type 2 is 24 bits per pixel compressed and 32bpp once expanded ("24bit color
image, forced to 32bit fixed alpha"), and type 3 is 15 bits compressed and
16bpp expanded. These two tables are easy to conflate and lead in opposite
directions.

**This CLEARS our decoder rather than condemning it.** `sl_gfx_tex.h`'s comment
"RGB24 is stored 32bpp" describes the decompressed form, which is what the
decoder is handed - so it is right, and the self-test assertion
`rgb24 stride == rgba32` is right with it. Reading table #4 as the stored size
would have made both look wrong and produced a third bad patch.

**THE NOTES IDENTIFY THE IMAGE, AND IT IS RAW.** `imageTypes.txt` is a
per-image-ID inventory, and there are exactly two 5x12 images in the game -
IDs `08B7` (ROM B578EC) and `08B9` (ROM B57B31). Both are documented as:

    Greyscale TableOffsetter 0 [W05 H0C] 32-bit RAW RGBA Transparent?

**RAW** - uncompressed. So the 24-to-32 expansion theory above is dead: type 2
never enters into it, there is no expansion, and a raw image is essentially
copied from ROM to the texpool.

That is what makes the observation sharp. ROM data is big-endian, so a raw
RGBA32 image arrives with its bytes already in R,G,B,A order and reading them
positionally - which is what the decoder does - is CORRECT. Yet the texpool
holds `f5 0e 2f 53` where ROM order would give `53 2f 0e f5`. The bytes are
reversed somewhere between ROM and the pool.

**Two more candidates eliminated:**

- *A ROM-wide byte swap at load.* There is none. `sl_ultra_shim.c:317` reads
  the file verbatim with `fread` and no swap pass, and the DMA path's own
  comment states "DMA delivers ROM bytes verbatim; multi-byte header fields are
  big-endian".
- *A swap in the texture load path.* `grep` over image.c, image_bank.c and
  tex.c finds `sl_swap_words` only in image_bank.c, and only over the bank
  DECLARATIONS (the B-027 fix). Pixel data is never swapped there.

**Why compressed textures are unaffected, which is the clue worth keeping.**
Almost every other texture is compressed and goes through `texInflateZlib` /
`texInflateNonZlib`, which consume a bitstream and emit bytes - so their output
byte order is a property of the inflater, not of how the input words sit in
memory. A RAW image is the only kind that inherits whatever order the copy
produced. That also explains why 8-bit fonts stay legible and the crosshair
looks perfect while this one icon is wrong: nothing else in frame takes the raw
path.

**THE NEXT MEASUREMENT, and it is decisive.** Dump the ROM bytes at 0xB578EC
(image 08B7) and compare them against the texpool bytes at the address
`tconfig->index` points to. If ROM reads `53 2f 0e f5` and the pool reads
`f5 0e 2f 53`, the reversal is inside the raw-copy path and that path is the
fix site. If ROM ALSO reads `f5 0e 2f 53`, then the pool is faithful and the
inventory's "32-bit RAW RGBA" is not how this particular image is stored - in
which case the declaration's own format nibbles decide it, and the decoder is
being handed the wrong format rather than the wrong bytes.

**Where it actually stands.** `texLoad` patches the declaration's `index` field
in place with a texpool address (image.c:2476). The next measurement is to
compare the bytes at that address against the image's own ROM data - if they
are byte-reversed there, the fault is in the load/decompress path for this
image, and `dxt=512` (against the crosshair's `dxt=128`) is the clue worth
following, since dxt selects the loadblock behaviour. Entry 140 of the
same dump is a 32x32 RGBA32 texture from the same frame - the crosshair - and it
decodes to a clean red reticle. Same format, same code path, same run. So
`SL_TEX_RGBA32` handling and channel order are not at fault, and the icon's
texels are simply not the icon's texels.

That moves the search out of the renderer entirely and into texture LOADING.
The declaration's `index` field is patched in place by `texLoad` to a texpool
address (image.c:2476), so the candidates are now: the icon never got
decompressed into the pool, it was decompressed to a different address than the
one patched in, or it was overwritten afterwards. Note entry 150 carries
`dxt=512` where the crosshair carries `dxt=128`, and dxt is a loadblock
parameter - worth checking whether this image takes a different load path.

Comparing the bytes at the patched address against the image's ROM data is the
next measurement, and it is decisive either way. Magenta is R and B high with G
low, which is the shape a channel-order error takes - worth testing against a
known-good RGBA32 texture from the same frame before anything else, since
several other `fmt=0` entries decode in the same run and could be compared.

**Two dump-tooling bugs fixed while getting here, both of which HID the icon:**
the dump cap was 96 and the run produced 192 entries, and the filename builder
used two digits so anything past entry 99 collided and was never written. Entry
150 - the icon - was invisible to both. Cap raised to 512, ids widened to three
digits. Worth noting the cap had ALREADY been raised once (12 -> 96) for
exactly this reason; a silent limit in a diagnostic tool costs more than the
bug it hides.

The draw is `microcode_generation_ammo_related` (gunfire.c:5825), reached from
`generate_ammo_total_microcode` via `set_rgba_redirect_generate_microcode`. It
sets `gDPSetTextureLUT(G_TT_NONE)` among its state, which is worth checking
first against what `gbi_to_sl_fmt` does with `tlut == 0` for a paletted source -
the icon comes from `ammo_related[ammotype].IconImage`, a global image bank
declaration, and the bank's byte fields were exactly what B-027 repaired.

**A DIFFERENT bug was found and fixed on the way, and it is NOT this one.**
`set_rgba_redirect_generate_microcode` is declared `Gfx *` and had NO return
statement - it called through and fell off the end, while its caller assigned
the result to `gdl`. On MIPS the callee's return value is still in v0 at the
epilogue so it flows through, and the ROM depends on that; x86 offers no such
guarantee. Guarded and returned properly natively.

It changed nothing: captures before and after are byte-identical (RMSE 0), so
GCC happened to leave the value in eax as well. Kept anyway - relying on a
register surviving a fall-through is undefined behaviour that any optimisation
change could break - but recorded as a latent-bug guard rather than a fix,
because claiming otherwise would be false. It is also the ONLY returnless
`Gfx *` function in gunfire.c or bondview2.c, so that class is closed.

**Also still unreproduced: the in-game health gauge.** `SL_TOUGH=0.4` starts
Bond at 40% health (player.c:497) but the gauge did not draw in any captured
frame, so B-035's symptom still has no headless reproduction. The watch-menu
ring remains confirmed correct. Getting the IN-GAME gauge on screen is the
blocker for that one.

### B-042 — hang in chrCreateBloodStain: PointUsage contents never swapped — FIXED

Caught by the frame watchdog in the owner's own session, which named it
outright:

```
kind: HANG   frame 0x1f1d
  chrCreateBloodStain            chr.c:3309
  chrHandleBulletHit             chr.c:3606
  chraiDefaultWeaponFireHandler  chrprop.c:1089
```

Shooting a guard hung the game. `chrCreateBloodStain` walks a chain through the
point-usage table - `index = PointUsage[index]` until index goes negative - and
unswapped s16 indices sent it somewhere wrong, where it could cycle forever.

**The gap was known and written down.** `sl_swap_model.c` swapped the POINTER
to the table with the rest of the record but never its CONTENTS, and the file's
own header listed "PointUsage tables (count not yet confirmed)" as unfinished.
The missing piece was the length.

**The notes supplied it**, from `Display Lists and Object Generation/Objects/
Point Merging.txt`: "Usage tables have one entry for each point in the display
list's point table." Its worked example is a piece documented as having "2E
normal points" whose usage table holds exactly 0x2E entries. So the length is
`numVertices`, one s16 per vertex - which also keeps the write inside the table.

**Measured before and after.** At the swap entry the raw values are 2816, 2560,
1792, 1536, 4352, 19968 - every one of the form 0xNN00, small indices with
their bytes reversed. Swapped they read 11, 10, 7, 6, 17, 78. Across a boot:
120 tables, 4236 entries, **2095 of them non-terminator and therefore actively
wrong before this fix**.

**Why it hid, and it is the third time this exact shape has appeared.** The
chain terminates on a negative value and 0xFFFF is byte-order invariant, so a
fully-wrong table still LOOKS correctly terminated. B-037 (the waypoint BFS)
and B-032 (the display-list walk) both hid the same way. Any list walked to a
negative sentinel is now a place to check first.

**Verified:** 16000-frame replay through the real render path, no hang; the
swap measured firing on real data as above; `make matching` MATCH!
byte-identical; `make bootsweep` 20/20.

Honest limit: the replay does not prove the blood-stain path was re-exercised,
so the strong evidence is the value measurement rather than the clean run.

### B-043 — face visible inside Bond's head: FIXED — the renderer discarded ENV alpha

**The owner supplied the mechanism by watching the original:** Bond's model
FADES AWAY as the level-start camera enters the back of his head. That is how
Rare hid it - not culling. Recording this because it redirected the whole
investigation: B-040 spent a day on back-face culling, which was the wrong
mechanism AND broke every character model when enabled.

The machinery is all present and correct. `currentPlayerStartChrFade` /
`currentPlayerTickChrFade` (bondview2.c:4240-4277) ramp `chr->fadealpha`, which
`chrRenderProp` (chr.c:2895) honours, and the trigger at bondview2.c:1381 even
carries the decomp's own comment: "Fade player body from opaque to transparent
just before the player takes control."

**Measured, and it is a one-tick boundary:**

```
call 1  tick 362  bondviewSetCameraMode     (:818)   duration=0   target=1.0
call 2  tick 533  bondviewFrozenCameraTick  (:1383)  duration=30  target=0.0
call 3  tick 562  bondviewAdvanceCameraMode (:1037)  duration=0   target=1.0
```

The intro fade DOES fire, correctly, with the right duration and target. It is
then cancelled 29 ticks later by a `duration=0, target=1.0` call that snaps the
model straight back to opaque - one tick before the 30-tick fade would have
completed, and at exactly the moment the camera is inside the head.

Note call 3's site is the one the decomp annotates "What's the point of this
call?" - its authors found it odd too.

**Why it is inherently one short.** The trigger is
`if (sp30 < 30.0f && sp30 + delta >= 30.0f)`, and sp30 steps down by exactly
`delta` (measured: 44, 43, 42 ... stepping 1.0 with delta 1.0). At sp30 == 30
the `<` test is false, so the earliest it can fire is sp30 == 29 - leaving 29
ticks for a 30-tick fade.

**FULL CHAIN TRACED. The fade alpha is computed, stored, and then never read.**

Measured end to end:

1. `chr->fadealpha` ramps correctly - 29 writes, 246 238 229 221 212 204 195 187...
2. `chrRenderProp` skips the faded model in the opaque pass and draws it in the
   alpha pass with render-mode type 3. BOTH passes run: 3547 calls each, and the
   faded branch is reached 295 times in each. The alpha pass is NOT missing.
3. `chr.c:2996` ORs the alpha into the low byte of the render data's env
   colour - executed 28 times, with `envcol before = 0x5a000000`, so it lands.
4. `modelApplyRenderModeType3` (model.c:3501) then reads it back... from the
   WRONG FIELD:

```c
if (renderdata->PropType == PROP_TYPE_VIEWER+1) {
    if (isPrimary) { r,g,b,a  from fogcolour; }     /* measured: ALWAYS this */
    else           { r,g,b from envcolour; a = 0xFF; }
```

Every sampled call has `PropType=7` (VIEWER+1) and `isPrimary=1`, so it takes
the fogcolour branch. `fogcolour` measured a constant `0x0b160bb4` throughout -
the level's fog, not a ramp. The fade alpha sits in `envcolour`'s low byte and
is never read.

**So the question is why `isPrimary` is 1 for this draw.** The two call sites
are model.c:4123 (`isPrimary=1`) and model.c:4138 (`isPrimary=0`), selected by
NODE TYPE - DLPRIMARY versus DL. If this tree classifies Bond's nodes as
primary where the ROM would not, the fade is discarded exactly as observed.
That is the next measurement: which node type the viewer's model presents, and
whether the same node reaches 4138 on the matching ROM.

**Note the non-primary branch hardcodes `a = 0xFF`.** So even reaching it does
not obviously deliver the ramp - worth understanding before assuming the fix is
simply to flip the branch. Do not patch either site until the node
classification is measured; three plausible-but-wrong fixes have already come
out of this bug.

**Candidates ELIMINATED, so nobody re-runs them:** the fade machinery, the
trigger, the ramp, the stored alpha, the missing-alpha-pass theory, and the
one-tick timing shortfall (inherent arithmetic, ~3% opacity, not a defect).

**THE FADE WORKS. Measured at bondview2.c:4274, 29 writes ramping:**

```
tick 1: frac=0.967 -> 246      tick 6: frac=0.800 -> 204
tick 2: frac=0.933 -> 238      tick 9: frac=0.700 -> 178
tick 3: frac=0.900 -> 229     tick 12: frac=0.600 -> 153
```

`fadealpha` is `u8` and the `(s8)` cast round-trips correctly through it, so the
stored values are right. So the machinery, the trigger, the ramp and the stored
alpha are ALL correct, and the model still draws solid.

**Which moves this out of the fade entirely and into the RENDERER.**
`chrRenderProp` (chr.c:2903) branches on the fade:

```c
if ((chrfadealpha < 0xFF) || (chr->chrflags & CHRFLAG_00020000)) {
    if (withalpha == 0) ...
```

A faded character belongs to a separate ALPHA PASS - `chrpropRender` takes
`withalpha` and the game draws the world in two passes. If the alpha pass never
runs natively, or runs without blending, a fading model draws at full opacity
and the fade is invisible no matter how correct its alpha is. That is the same
shape as B-026, where four separate symptoms turned out to be one missing blend
state.

**Next step: count the two passes.** Instrument `chrpropRender` and record how
often it is called with `withalpha != 0` versus `== 0` during the intro. If the
alpha pass never runs, that is the bug and it is nothing to do with timing.

**The one-tick shortfall below is probably NOT a defect.** Trigger at 29
remaining, duration 30, camera advance at 0 remaining - the arithmetic is
inherent and would hold on hardware too. 29/30 of the fade still reaches ~3%
opacity, which is invisible in practice. Do not chase it until the alpha pass
is ruled out.

**Do NOT "fix" this by lengthening the fade or loosening the comparison.** Both
are Rare's code and rule 5 applies. The real question is which side has drifted
natively: the trigger firing a tick late, or `bondviewAdvanceCameraMode`
arriving a tick early. `g_GlobalTimerDelta` measured exactly 1.000 throughout,
so the intro tick accounting is the place to look - compare the tick at which
the camera advances against the emulator running the matching ROM, where the
same instrumentation can be applied to a build that is byte-identical to the
one Rare shipped.

That comparison is the next step and it is decisive: it says whether our timing
is wrong or the fade genuinely completes on hardware with a different count.

**Earlier measurement corrected.** An initial sample showed `fadealpha` pinned
at 255 and I read that as "the fade never runs". It samples every 200 draws and
simply missed the window; the fade runs and is reverted.

## B-043 RESOLVED (2026-08-26). The starting question was mis-posed.

**Status:** fixed in `src/gfx/sl_gfx_dl.c` (native renderer only; the matching
build does not compile this file). Uncommitted, in the working tree.

### The `isPrimary` question above has no answer, because it rests on two
### mistakes. Recording both, because each felt solid from the inside.

**Mistake 1 — "the two call sites are selected by NODE TYPE, DLPRIMARY vs DL".**
They are not. model.c:4123 and model.c:4138 are both inside
`modelRenderNodeGundl`, and they are the SAME node's `rodata->Primary` and
`rodata->Secondary` display lists. `isPrimary` distinguishes a node's two
surface lists, not two kinds of node. (The other pair, model.c:4307/4324, is
the same shape inside `modelRenderNodeDl`.) There was never a node
classification to measure.

**Mistake 2, and the load-bearing one — a faded character never reaches the
`VIEWER+1` branch at all.** `chrRenderProp` (chr.c:2993-3001):

```c
if (chrfadealpha < 0xFF) { mrData.PropType = 8; mrData.envcolour.word |= (u8)chrfadealpha; }
else                     { mrData.PropType = 7; }
```

`PROP_TYPE` (src/bondconstants.h:3866-3877) is NUL,OBJ,DOOR,CHR,WEAPON,PLAYER,
VIEWER,EXPLOSION,SMOKE — so `VIEWER+1` is 7 and `EXPLOSION+1` is 8. The two
values are set by the same `if` that decides whether there is a fade at all.
**7 is the not-fading case.** The earlier sample that found "PropType=7 always"
was sampling non-faded characters; it never caught the fade window, so it
measured the wrong branch and the `a = 0xFF` beside it was a red herring.

The branch a fading character DOES take — `PROP_TYPE_EXPLOSION+1`,
model.c:3547 (Type3) and model.c:3834 (Type4) — reads the alpha out of
`envcolour`'s low byte exactly as intended. **The game code is correct and
always was.** Every candidate inside `src/game/` is now eliminated.

### Where it actually broke: the native display-list interpreter.

Measured, not read. Telemetry on `tri_alpha` (`sl_gfx_dl.c:2097`) over a
Facility boot, `SL_BOOT_LEVEL=34 SL_FRAMES=1700` under `xvfb-run`:

```
frame 421   envscale tris=516     env-a 255..255
frame 541   envscale tris=18528   env-a 187..246
frame 601   envscale tris=62328   env-a 16..246     <- and never rises again
```

A ramping env alpha DOES reach geometry, on 61320 triangles, stepping 246 down
to 16 — and confined entirely to frames 482-601, the intro window. Only ONE
distinct combiner produced any of it, `fc159a04 5ffefff8`, decoded against
`include/PR/gbi.h:3145-3159` (GCCc0w0/GCCc0w1, which is also what
`sl_gfx_dl.c`'s existing FC classifier reads):

```
cycle 0 rgb   (TEXEL0 - ENVIRONMENT) * SHADE_ALPHA + ENVIRONMENT
cycle 0 alpha (TEXEL0 - 0) * ENVIRONMENT + 0
cycle 1 alpha (0 - 0) * 0 + COMBINED
```

That is `modelApplyRenderModeType3`'s `EXPLOSION+1` branch, character for
character. So the fade survives all the way into the display list.

**And then `tri_alpha` throws it away:**

```c
static unsigned char tri_alpha(const struct vtx *v)
{
    if (g_cc_a_prim) return g_prim[3];
    return v->a;                          /* ENV is never consulted */
}
```

The FC classifier tracked PRIMITIVE alpha and TEXEL0 alpha and never
ENVIRONMENT. `OP_SETENVCOL` loaded `g_env[3]` faithfully; nothing read it.
Every faded triangle drew at vertex alpha, which measurement (below) shows is
255 on every single one of them. Same shape as B-026 and B-034: the command was
CONSUMED, not INTERPRETED.

### The fix

`sl_gfx_dl.c`, three places, all native-only:

1. `OP_SETCOMBINE` gains `g_cc_a_envscale` — true only when the cycle-0 alpha
   is the restricted form `(a - 0) * ENVIRONMENT + 0`, i.e. `Ac0 == ENV` and
   `Ab0`/`Ad0` are both the "0" mux (7, `G_ACMUX_0`). That is the only shape
   whose result is a plain SCALE of `a`, so it is the only one a
   classify-don't-emulate path can carry exactly. Deliberately narrow: the
   `VIEWER+1` branch beside it spells `(TEXEL0 - ENV) * SHADE + ENV`, which
   also names ENV but is not a scale, and must keep drawing as it does.
2. `tri_alpha` honours it, taking the `a` term from `Aa0` and scaling by
   `g_env[3]`. For `Aa0 == TEXEL0` the base is 255 because GL_MODULATE already
   multiplies the texture's own alpha into `glColor`'s — so the returned env
   alpha reproduces `TEXEL0.a * ENV.a` exactly, not approximately.
3. A report line, `sl_cc: env-scaled-alpha tris=N`, so a future session can see
   at a glance whether this path fired.

**The one design ambiguity was settled by measurement, not by argument.** The
alternative was "scale the PREVIOUS return value by env" (`v->a * env`) rather
than "take the base from the a-mux". These differ only when vertex alpha is
below 255 on such a draw. Probed across two levels:

```
facility  vtx-a 255=62328/62328   a-src mux TEXEL0=62328  SHADE=0  1=0
statue    vtx-a 255=18900/18900   a-src mux TEXEL0=18900  SHADE=0  1=0
```

100% and 100%. The two formulations are indistinguishable on all real data, so
the ambiguity is empirically absent; the faithful reading of the RDP equation
was kept.

### Verification — what was actually run

**The captured frame, which is the thing that was asked for.** Facility,
`xvfb-run -a --server-args="-screen 0 640x480x24" env SL_ROM=baserom.u.z64
SL_BOOT_LEVEL=34 SL_WINDOW=1 SL_FRAMES=1700 SL_SHOT=... SL_SHOT_EVERY=25`,
identical runs before and after:

- Before: shot 22 is Bond's face filling the screen, fully opaque, seen from
  inside the head.
- After: the same frame draws the head translucent — the door struts behind it
  read through the face — and at 4-frame cadence the ramp is visible running
  from solid, through translucent, to gone, before the player takes control.

**Blast radius, measured rather than argued.** Per-frame `compare -metric RMSE`
across all 34 shots of the two Facility runs: **exactly one frame differs** —
shot 22, the head passthrough. All 33 others are RMSE 0, bit-identical.

**The change was verified on the path it touches (character geometry), not on
room geometry** — the B-040 trap. Two further levels captured under both
binaries at 8-frame cadence, 82 shots each:

- **streets (29):** 3 frames differ, and they are the same intro-camera head
  passthrough, fixed the same way. The fix GENERALIZES; it is not a Facility
  special case.
- **statue (22):** 22 frames differ, all at low RMSE (22-300, against 18443 for
  the head). Located the changed pixels exactly and looked at them: they are the
  ornate iron gate in the background, a prop drawn through the same
  `(a-0)*ENV+0` alpha shape, now correctly slightly see-through. Bond's model in
  the foreground is untouched in every one of those frames.

`grep -rn "PropType = " src/game/*.c` over the whole tree: `PropType = 8` is set
in exactly ONE place, chr.c:2995. Nothing else in the game can reach the branch
this change affects.

Gates:

```
make matching                MATCH!   EXIT=0
make bootsweep               20/20 OK  EXIT=0
make trace-verify LEVEL=facility   IDENTICAL - 15869 ticks match  EXIT=0
```

`src/gfx/sl_gfx_tex.c` was not touched, so its self-test was not required.
The binary rebuilt after the probe instrumentation was removed is
**byte-identical** to the one every frame above was captured with, so the
evidence applies to the tree as it stands.

### Still true, still not a defect

The 29-ticks-for-a-30-tick-fade shortfall recorded above is unchanged and was
not touched. Rule 5: it is Rare's arithmetic. It is visible in the captures as
the model still being near-solid for the first frame or two of the ramp, which
is what the original does too.

### What this cost, and the lesson worth keeping

Three wrong fixes came out of this bug before, and a fourth was avoided only
because the brief said to find the flaw before patching. The flaw was that
**the sample that established "PropType=7 always" never covered the window
where the bug happens.** A measurement taken outside the event proves nothing
about the event, and it is indistinguishable from a good measurement from the
inside — it has real numbers and a real call count. The guard that worked here
was correlating every counter with the FRAME RANGE it came from; the moment the
env-alpha telemetry was bucketed per frame, the window announced itself
(482-601) and the whole thing fell out in one run.
